3D & Gaussian Splatting

PhyGaP: Physically-Grounded Gaussians with Polarization Cues

The problem. Reconstructing glossy objects in 3D fails to decompose albedo (inherent color) from reflected light correctly. RGB images don't encode the surface normals, reflectance, and roughness needed to separate diffuse reflection from specular reflection, so when you try to relight a reconstructed object under different lighting, it shows color shifts and unrealistic shading.

The approach. Use polarized light images as input, since polarization carries information about how light bounces off surfaces. Build a physically-grounded rendering pipeline that models both polarization and reflection together, and add a technique to handle complex lighting in non-convex objects. The polarization cues directly constrain the surface properties, making the decomposition accurate enough for realistic relighting.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

PQDT: Pseudo-Query Dual Transformer for Robust Point Cloud Restoration

The problem. Point clouds in the real world are messy—they have missing patches, noise, outliers, and varying density all at once. Most restoration methods use a bottleneck: they squeeze all information through a single global code, which loses local geometric detail and breaks down when the input is corrupted. When you have multiple types of degradation together, existing methods struggle.

The approach. Split the restoration into two stages: first, generate pseudo-queries (intermediate geometric anchors) from the noisy input, stabilizing the coarse shape. Then refine those queries using learned shape priors that act as knowledge about what clean shapes should look like. The two stages alternate between trusting the input and trusting learned patterns, balancing local detail with global geometric plausibility.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Hg-I2P: Bridging Modalities for Generalizable Image-to-Point-Cloud Registration via Heterogeneous Graphs

Pei An, Junfeng Ding, Jiaqi Yang, Yulong Wang, Jie Ma, Liangliang Nan

The problem. When aligning 2D photos with 3D point clouds (a core task for robots locating themselves and reconstructing 3D scenes), the raw visual appearance of pixels and the geometric structure of 3D points live in completely different worlds. Even when you find a pixel that truly matches a 3D point, their features may look nothing alike because images show color and surface patterns while point clouds encode just raw shape. This massive gap between the two data types causes standard matching methods to fail when placed in new, unseen environments.

The approach. Instead of separately refining features and then filtering bad matches, treat the entire problem as a graph where 2D regions and 3D regions are nodes connected by edges. By letting information flow between regions across modalities—forcing the 2D and 3D sides to negotiate their features through these connections—the method teaches them to align better. At the same time, checking consistency within the graph structure (whether linked vertices agree) naturally eliminates bad correspondences. This unified view handles both feature quality and match reliability in one shot.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

InfiniDepth: Arbitrary-Resolution and Fine-Grained Depth Estimation with Neural Implicit Fields

Hao Yu, Haotong Lin, Jiawei Wang, Jiaxin Li, Yida Wang, Xueyang Zhang

The problem. Estimating depth (distance from the camera) from a single photo is hard enough, but standard methods are shackled by an even deeper constraint: they predict depth only at fixed grid positions matching the input image size. This means a method trained on 512×512 images produces blocky depth maps stuck at that same resolution and can never produce the fine geometric detail that lies between pixels. The blurry upsampling required to exceed training resolution loses critical surface details.

The approach. Instead of predicting depth on a rigid pixel grid, learn a continuous function that can answer 'what is the depth at any coordinate' anywhere in the image plane. Build this by querying features at multiple scales around a given coordinate, then feeding those aligned features into a small neural network to predict depth. Since the function is continuous, you can query it at any resolution, even higher than the training images, and naturally recover fine-grained geometric variations without blurring.

Generation

PDD: Manifold-Prior Diverse Distillation for Medical Anomaly Detection

The problem. Medical anomalies are subtle and scattered across complex anatomy, unlike sharp industrial defects. A single feature extractor can't capture this: CNNs excel at fine-grained textures but miss global structure, while sequence models see global patterns but not local detail. Existing teacher-student methods use homogeneous feature spaces that don't preserve representation diversity, hurting sensitivity to subtle abnormalities.

The approach. Use two frozen teacher networks with complementary strengths—a sequence model for global anatomy and a CNN for local texture—and align their heterogeneous features into a shared high-dimensional manifold. Distill this unified manifold into two structurally identical but functionally diverse students with different learning objectives: one focuses on local layer-wise consistency, the other on cross-layer dependencies. A diversity loss prevents them from collapsing into the same solution.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Repurposing 3D Generative Model for Autoregressive Layout Generation

Haoran Feng, Yifan Niu, Zehuan Huang, Yang-Tian Sun, Chunchao Guo, Yuxin Peng

The problem. Generating coherent 3D room layouts (placing furniture and objects so they don't collide and make spatial sense) is hard because language-based methods understand semantics ('dining table goes in the dining area') but often miss physical constraints, while 2D image optimization is computationally expensive and doesn't truly understand 3D geometry. The fundamental issue is that existing approaches don't operate in native 3D space where spatial relationships and physics constraints live naturally.

The approach. Leverage pre-trained 3D generative models (which already learned distributions of realistic spatial arrangements from massive 3D data) by repurposing them as an autoregressive generator: place one object at a time, conditioning on the current scene state and the instruction. This lets the model's built-in 3D prior automatically enforce physical plausibility. To prevent error accumulation across many sequential placements, combine scene-level guidance (is the whole room sensible?) with step-by-step refinement.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

BiProLoRA: Bilevel Prompt LoRA for Real Scene Recovery

Nan An, Long Ma, Tengyu Ma, Zhu Liu, Yingchi Liu, Risheng Liu

The problem. Large pre-trained generative models (like diffusion models) work great in the lab on clean synthetic images, but fail when deployed to real messy scenarios—low-light photos, hazy views, underwater video. The distribution of real degradations differs so much from synthetic training data that the model's learned distributions no longer match, and simple fine-tuning gets stuck overfitting to one type of degradation or losing the model's initial knowledge.

The approach. Adapt the model in two complementary stages: first, calibrate the model's internal representation to match the statistics of real degraded images without requiring full retraining. Second, combine two lightweight adaptation techniques (prompts for degradation-aware conditioning and LoRA for structure recovery) in a joint optimization loop where they mutually improve each other—prompts focus on understanding what degradation is present, while LoRA preserves structural knowledge. This balance enables the model to handle both seen and completely unseen degradations.

Vision-Language

SO-Bench: A Structural Output Evaluation of Multimodal LLM

Di Feng, Kaixin Ma, Feng Nan, Haofeng Chen, Bohan Zhai, David Griffiths

The problem. Multimodal language models are deployed as agents that must extract information from images and return it in exact JSON schema formats to control downstream systems and APIs. Current models often produce output that is semantically correct but violates schema rules—wrong nesting, missing fields, or extra properties. There is no benchmark that systematically measures how well models follow schemas grounded in visual evidence.

The approach. Build a benchmark dataset of 1,800 diverse image-schema pairs spanning UI screens, documents, charts, and natural images, each paired with a unique JSON schema and human-verified ground truth. Evaluate models on three dimensions: schema adherence (following the structure), structural fidelity (correct nesting and types), and value accuracy. This enables rigorous measurement of the gap between visual understanding and structured reasoning in multimodal models.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

AVION: Aerial Vision-Language Instruction from Offline Teacher to Prompt-Tuned Network

Yu Hu, Jianyang Gu, Hao Liu, Yue Cao, Jozsef Hamari, Zheng Liu

The problem. Adapting general vision-language models to aerial imagery (photos from drones or satellites taken top-down) is tricky because the same object class varies wildly depending on season, sensor, and altitude, yet training data only provides bare class names ('building', 'road'). Additionally, the visual encoder is frozen to save compute, so it can't adapt to these aerial-specific variations. Without addressing these two gaps—semantic poverty and visual rigidity—the model aligns text with the wrong visual patterns.

The approach. Use a frozen large teacher model to guide a lightweight student: have the teacher generate multiple descriptions for each class using a language model (enriching 'building' into concrete aerial variants), then filter these descriptions by asking which ones truly align with the visual data. Train the student with learnable prompts in both the vision and language encoders to internalize these semantically rich prototypes. This tri-aspect alignment (text, vision, and their matching logits) allows the student to capture aerial-specific visual diversity while staying efficient.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Progressive Cross-Modal Causal Intervention for Long-Term Action Recognition

Shaowu Xu, Xibin Jia, Chao Fan, Junyu Gao, Jing Chang, Qianmei Sun

The problem. Recognizing complex actions built from many sub-steps (like 'making scrambled eggs' from cracking eggs, heating butter, stirring, etc.) using vision-language models is tripped up by spurious correlations. The model might align the action label with a chef's hat or kitchen background rather than the actual causal actions, or it might confuse overlapping sub-steps across different activities. These illusions arise because the model relies on statistical co-occurrence rather than causal reasoning.

The approach. Apply causal interventions in three progressive stages: block co-occurrence hallucination by using optimal transport to isolate true action-visual features from frequently-co-occurring confounders; address codependency illusion by explicitly modeling semantic relationships among sub-actions (some are exclusive, some are shared); finally, apply front-door adjustment to remove remaining visual confounders by using the deconfounded text embeddings as a mediator. Each stage targets a different type of spurious correlation, building robust action recognition.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

SenseSearch: Empowering Vision-Language Models with High-Resolution Agentic Search-Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning

Yong Xien Chng, Tao Hu, Wenwen Tong, Xueheng Li, Jiandong Chen, Haojia Yu

The problem. Vision-language models struggle with knowledge-intensive questions about high-resolution images because they only carry static training knowledge and cannot zoom in to see fine details. While search tools and image cropping are useful, existing methods use them in isolation without learning when and how to combine them, and they lack the reasoning ability to plan multi-step investigations.

The approach. Train an agentic VLM using reinforcement learning to dynamically choose among three tools—text search (for factual information), image search (for reference images), and image crop (for fine-grained analysis)—as it reasons through a problem. Start with a small supervised dataset to teach basic tool usage, then use RL to learn optimal tool-sequencing strategies and reasoning chains. This allows the model to adaptively coordinate tools based on what it discovers at each step, similar to how humans investigate complex visual queries.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Video

Generalizable Video Quality Assessment via Weak-to-Strong Learning

Linhan Cao, Wei Sun, Xiangyang Zhu, et al.

The problem. Video quality assessment models trained on one dataset often fail on out-of-distribution videos from different cameras, compression, or frame rates. Creating large human-annotated datasets for quality assessment is expensive and time-consuming due to strict experimental standards required by international telecom guidelines. The field is stuck: models generalize poorly, but scaling up annotation is prohibitively costly.

The approach. Instead of training on human-annotated labels, use existing imperfect VQA models as weak teachers to train stronger student models on unlabeled data. Combine multiple weak teachers (both other VQA models and synthetic distortion simulators) through ranking, so the student learns from diverse signals while filtering out their individual biases. Then recycle each trained student as the teacher for the next iteration, progressively focusing on hard examples that previous teachers couldn't predict.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

GEM: Generating LiDAR World Model via Deformable Mamba

Yang Wu, Zhaojiang Liu, Qiang Meng, Youquan Liu, Renliang Weng, Jianjun Qian

The problem. LiDAR world models must predict future sensor observations for autonomous driving, but point clouds are unstructured and lack texture cues. Converting them to regular representations (voxels or bird's-eye-view images) loses geometric precision. Point clouds also tangle dynamic objects with static scenery, making it hard to model what will move versus what stays, so previous models produce temporally inconsistent predictions.

The approach. Align LiDAR's sequential scanning structure with Mamba's sequential processing to preserve geometric detail naturally. First tokenize LiDAR sweeps into compact codes. Then explicitly disentangle dynamic objects from static geometry without manual labels, separating what will change from what won't. Finally use a multi-path deformable Mamba to process both branches in parallel and fuse them with adaptive gating, enabling temporal consistency and optional autonomous rollout.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Wavelet-based Frame Selection by Detecting Semantic Boundary for Long Video Understanding

Wang Chen, Yuhui Zeng, Yongdong Luo, Tianyu Xie, Luojun Lin, Jiayi Ji

The problem. Applying large vision-language models to long videos hits a practical wall: you cannot feed all frames due to computational limits, so you must select a subset. Current methods pick frames with highest relevance to a query, but this produces scattered frames that destroy the narrative flow—like understanding a movie by watching random beautiful shots rather than its plot. Missing semantic transitions means the model cannot reason about process or causality.

The approach. Reframe the problem: instead of just selecting high-relevance frames, first detect where the story's 'chapters' change by treating the frame-relevance signal as a noisy time series and applying wavelet decomposition to isolate meaningful semantic shifts from noise. Identify chapter boundaries where these transitions peak, segmenting the video into coherent clips. Then allocate frames proportionally to each segment's importance and select diverse, relevant frames within each—preserving both narrative structure and individual relevance.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

LEMON: A Large Endoscopic MONocular Dataset and Foundation Model for Perception in Surgical Settings

Chengan Che, Chao Wang, Tom Vercauteren, Sophia Tsoka, Luis C. Garcia-Peraza-Herrera

The problem. Building computer vision systems for surgical perception requires massive, diverse video data, but collecting high-quality annotated surgical videos is prohibitively expensive—existing datasets have fewer than 100 videos totaling dozens of hours. Foundation models need scale to generalize across diverse surgeries, instruments, and surgical techniques, yet the practical and privacy barriers to data collection have kept the field severely bottlenecked.

The approach. Aggregate surgical videos from publicly available YouTube sources at scale using an automated pipeline: classify videos to confirm surgical content, filter frames to remove non-surgical segments, and leverage language models to auto-label procedure types. This yields a massive foundation dataset (938 hours, 4000+ videos). Pre-train a foundation model on this diverse data using self-supervised learning with knowledge distillation, then fine-tune it on downstream surgical tasks. The scale enables the model to generalize across procedures where smaller datasets fail.

Perception

Focus on Background: Exploring SAM's Potential in Few-shot Medical Image Segmentation

Yuntian Bo, Yazhou Zhu, Piotr Koniusz, Haofeng Zhang

The problem. SAM, a capable segmentation model trained on natural images, over-segments medical images because it struggles with low-contrast, ambiguous boundaries between adjacent organs and tissues. Existing methods give SAM foreground prompts (the target anatomy), but these alone don't constrain over-segmentation. No one has focused on the background—the tissue just outside the boundary that should act as a constraint.

The approach. Reframe the segmentation task as background point localization. Extract support images showing where the target anatomy is, then directly predict where background points should lie near the boundary—not as semantic regions but as strategic locations. Use contextual modeling to capture how background and foreground spatially relate, and add structural constraints so predicted background points respect the expected spatial patterns in medical images. This gives SAM precise guidance without relying on semantic background labels.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

RAID: Retrieval-Augmented Anomaly Detection

Mingxiu Cai, Zhe Zhang, Gaochang Wu, Tianyou Chai, Xiatian Zhu

The problem. Detecting manufacturing defects without any anomaly samples (unsupervised learning) typically involves either reconstructing normal patterns from memory or comparing test images to templates, but both suffer from noisy matching—misaligned template retrieval or imperfect reconstructions produce false alarms and miss subtle defects. Template-based methods also struggle when adapting to new product categories with few or no normal reference images.

The approach. Apply the retrieval-augmented generation paradigm: instead of relying only on single best-matching templates, retrieve multiple normal exemplars at varying levels (class-level prototypes, semantic clusters, individual patches) in a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. Compute a matching cost volume between the test patch and all retrieved exemplars, then use a guided mixture-of-experts network that leverages both the retrieved patterns and their semantic relationships to suppress matching noise and generate clean anomaly maps. This reduces hallucinations and generalizes better to unseen anomaly types.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

FastRef: Fast Prototype Refinement for Few-shot Industrial Anomaly Detection

Yufei Li, Long Tian, Yuyang Dai, Wenchao Chen, Liang Bao, Xiyang Liu

The problem. Few-shot anomaly detection (identifying defects from just 1–4 normal samples) is challenging because prototypes built from so few images are weak and don't capture the full range of normal variation. At inference, test images carry information about what 'normal' looks like for this specific product, but existing methods ignore these query-image statistics when refining prototypes, leaving them suboptimal and susceptible to noise in the limited data.

The approach. Iteratively refine prototypes by drawing characteristics from query images: use optimal transport to understand which features of the query could transfer to enhance prototypes (characteristic transfer) while simultaneously preventing anomalies in the query from contaminating the refined prototypes (anomaly suppression). Balance these two constraints in a nested optimization loop resolved efficiently using Sinkhorn iterations and closed-form solutions, enabling real-time inference while significantly boosting detection with minimal data.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

From Infusion to Assimilation Distillation for Medical Image Segmentation

Jiankang Hong, Ye Luo, Yinan Liu, Junsong Yuan

The problem. Knowledge distillation—teaching a small, efficient student model from a large teacher—promises faster medical image segmentation, but many distillation approaches unexpectedly degrade the student's ability to generalize to new datasets. The problem is that standard distillation forces alignment on teacher-student features and predictions without accounting for the fact that student and teacher have different learning advantages; the student loses useful capabilities while absorbing teacher knowledge.

The approach. Use a two-stage distillation: first, infuse teacher knowledge through soft-label guidance combined with prototype alignment (calibrating class predictions and handling class imbalance). Second, assimilate this knowledge adaptively by using contrastive learning to refine predictions based on positive-negative sample relationships within the student's own learned features, plus reverse constraints that reinforce feature consistency. This allows the student to internalize and adapt teacher knowledge rather than blindly imitate it, preserving its own useful specificity.

Embodied / driving

A Unified Perspective on Adversarial Membership Manipulation in Vision Models

Zitao Gao, Huiting Hu, Lifeng Jiang, Ruoxi Jia, Bo Li

The problem. Privacy audits use membership inference attacks (MIAs) to detect if a specific image was in a model's training data, verifying data protection and compliance. But MIAs assume inputs are honest—no one has asked whether tiny imperceptible perturbations can fool them into falsely claiming a non-member image was actually used for training. This creates a vulnerability in the auditing process itself.

The approach. Show that non-member images can be adversarially perturbed to enter high-confidence regions where MIAs report membership. Uncover a geometric signature—the gradient norm progressively collapses as perturbations push samples toward these regions—that separates true members from fabricated ones despite similar semantics. Use this gradient-geometry signal to detect fabricated members and build robust MIAs resistant to input-space attacks.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

EnergyAction: Unimanual to Bimanual Composition with Energy-Based Models

Mingchen Song, Xiang Deng, Jie Wei, Dongmei Jiang, Liqiang Nie, Weili Guan

The problem. Training robots for two-handed tasks is prohibitively expensive because collecting dual-arm demonstrations requires sophisticated teleoperation systems and substantially more human effort than single-arm demonstrations. Yet single-arm skills exist in abundance. The challenge is that bimanual action spaces are exponentially larger and require precise temporal and spatial coordination (arms cannot collide), making it hard to learn from scratch.

The approach. Model individual single-arm policies as energy functions, where lower energy corresponds to more likely actions. Energy-based models have a compositional property: the joint distribution of two independent systems is their energy sum. Compose left and right arm policies by adding their energies, then constrain the resulting bimanual actions to satisfy temporal coherence (smooth, synchronized motions) and spatial feasibility (collision avoidance via inverse kinematics). This decomposes the complex bimanual problem into simpler single-arm components while enforcing physical constraints through energy penalties.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

LEAD: Minimizing Learner–Expert Asymmetry in End-to-End Driving

Long Nguyen, Micha Fauth, Bernhard Jaeger, Daniel Dauner, Maximilian Igl, Andreas Geiger

The problem. Teaching autonomous driving policies through imitation learning from privileged expert simulators works in theory, but in practice the student policy plateaus well below expert performance. The gap stems from three asymmetries: the expert 'sees' through occlusions and around corners that the student's cameras cannot; the expert knows precise velocities and accelerations while the student must infer from noisy observations; and the expert follows a dense route while the student only sees a single waypoint, making multi-step maneuvers ambiguous.

The approach. Redesign both the expert demonstrations and the student policy to reduce these asymmetries: constrain the expert to behave based only on what the student's sensors could observe and using only realistic sensor noise; add uncertainty awareness to the expert's decision-making. Strengthen the student's navigation conditioning by providing richer intent information early in the model (not just a single target point) and injecting it earlier in the architecture so perception features can interact with navigation before the decoder. These changes make expert behavior teachable.

Learning foundations

NuWa: Deriving Lightweight Class-Specific Vision Transformers for Edge Devices

Ziteng Wei, Qiang He, Bing Li, Feifei Chen, Hai Jin, Yun Yang

The problem. Vision Transformers need compression for edge devices, but existing pruning methods compress for all classes equally. Edge devices only care about specific classes—a smart vehicle only needs to recognize vehicles and pedestrians, not flowers. General compression wastes capacity on irrelevant knowledge and loses accuracy. Worse, class-specific pruning is slow: creating customized models for each device and class combination requires expensive retraining cycles.

The approach. Identify and remove class-detrimental weights—parameters that actively hurt performance on target classes (counterintuitively, sometimes pruning makes class-specific accuracy better). Use self-knowledge purification to find these weights without retraining, then formulate remaining pruning as closed-form optimization problems with analytical solutions, eliminating the need for iterative retraining. This trades one expensive training cycle for lightweight closed-form derivation of many custom models.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Hist2Style: Histogram-Guided Stylization with Bilateral Grids

Dekel Galor, Adam Pikielny, Zhoutong Zhang, Ke Wang, Laura Waller, Jiawen Chen

The problem. Automating color and tone adjustment (stylization) is hard: large generative models are slow, hallucinate details, and let users only control style via vague prompts. You can't precisely say 'make it 10% more saturated' or 'shift shadows toward blue.' Traditional photorealistic style transfer is too rigid. The field needs a method that's fast, prevents hallucinations, and gives users direct, intuitive control over color without distorting content.

The approach. Distill a large image editing model into a lightweight network trained on synthetic stylization pairs. Constrain all edits to locally affine color transforms via bilateral grids—a technique from computational photography that preserves edges. Condition the network on the histogram of the target style image, making color control interpretable: users can directly edit the histogram rather than writing prompts. This guarantees photorealism by construction and enables real-time, high-resolution editing.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

RevINN: An End-to-End Invertible Neural Network for Reversible Adversarial Examples

Jielun Huang, Chi-Man Pun, Guoheng Huang

The problem. Creating 'reversible adversarial examples'—images that fool deep networks into misclassification but can be restored to originals for authorized users—currently requires a two-stage process: generate adversarial noise, then embed that noise into the adversarial example for recovery. This decoupling causes quality loss: the carefully optimized adversarial perturbations get disrupted by the embedding step, reducing both attack strength and visual quality compared to non-reversible adversarial examples.

The approach. Use invertible neural networks to generate reversible adversarial examples in a single end-to-end stage. Decompose images into frequency components using wavelets, then apply bidirectional cross-frequency modulation: exchange discriminative information between low and high frequencies to create adversariality, with fine-grained modulation across high-frequency bands to strengthen the attack. Since wavelet operations and all network modules are reversible, the original image can be recovered without needing explicit perturbation embedding, eliminating the quality degradation of two-stage approaches.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Learning Mutual View Information Graph for Adaptive Adversarial Collaborative Perception

Yihang Tao, Senkang Hu, Haonan An, Zhengru Fang, Hangcheng Cao, Yuguang Fang

The problem. Autonomous vehicles sharing sensor data for collaborative perception are vulnerable to adversarial attacks where a malicious vehicle injects false detections. Existing defenses use consensus validation—comparing detections across vehicles—but they implicitly leak information about which regions are well-observed versus uncertain. Attackers can exploit this leaked confidence information to identify optimal times and locations for fabricating objects while evading detection.

The approach. Model the mutual view information of all vehicles as a temporal graph where nodes represent perceived regions and edges capture shared visibility and confidence patterns. Learn how this graph evolves over time to identify regions where vulnerability consensus makes attacks most likely to succeed. Use entropy-aware search to optimize when (which frames) and where (which regions) to attack, finding the most defensible-blind spots. This unified representation enables adaptive attacks that generalize across different defense mechanisms by learning their disclosed vulnerabilities.

Frontier / science

TopoSlide: Topologically-Informed Histopathology Whole Slide Image Representation Learning

Shahira Abousamra, Asmita Sood, Sylvia Plevritis

The problem. Whole slide images (WSIs) of cancer tissue are gigapixel-scale—too large to process as single images. Existing foundation models break them into thousands of patches, extract features per patch, then aggregate with pooling, which loses spatial relationships. Pathologists rely on how tissue regions are organized—where tumor clusters are, how immune cells are distributed—but current models don't explicitly capture this global organization.

The approach. Use persistent homology (a topological data analysis technique) to characterize the spatial arrangement of tissue clusters. First cluster the patch embeddings to identify histologically meaningful regions (solid tumors, glandular structures, etc.), then compute topological features: connected components describe how regions are distributed, and loops describe organizational patterns. Train a vision transformer to predict this topology from the whole-slide embedding, forcing the model to learn that global tissue architecture, not just local patches, matters for diagnosis.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Orthogonal Spatial-Aware Multi-View Anchor Graph Clustering for Incomplete Remote Sensing Image Data

Zhang et al.

The problem. Remote sensing data combines multiple sensor views (hyperspectral, multispectral, radar) for better Earth observation. Clustering pixels into land-cover categories from multiple views works well when all data is present, but real sensors fail—clouds block images, sensors malfunction, and data goes missing. Existing incomplete-data clustering methods ignore the spatial structure and spectral coherence that remote sensing data inherently has.

The approach. Build multi-scale anchor graphs initialized from superpixel segmentation, which preserves spatial texture patterns for each view. Learn complete graphs from incomplete data using view weighting and matrix factorization, so each view contributes according to how much data it has. Align the multi-scale graph structures into a shared feature space for consensus, then add spatial regularization in horizontal and vertical directions to enforce smoothness. This jointly optimizes for spectral-spatial coherence and robustness to missing data.

official paper (CVF) ↗ · code ↗ · © the authors, CVPR 2026

Cross-Scale Pansharpening via ScaleFormer and the PanScale Benchmark

Cao et al.

The problem. Fusing high-resolution panchromatic satellite images with low-resolution multi-spectral images to create high-resolution color maps is useful for agriculture and environmental monitoring, but existing methods are trained on small 256×256 crops and fail catastrophically when applied to real satellite images at 1600+ pixels due to memory blowup, tiling artifacts, and distribution shift between training resolution and real-world scales.

The approach. Reframe the resolution generalization problem as sequence-length generalization: use fixed-size image patches as stationary tokens, so varying image sizes only change the number of tokens, not individual token statistics. Train with variable effective sequence lengths via bucketed sampling to expose the model to different scales. Decouple spatial feature learning within patches from sequential dependencies between patches, using positional encoding that can extrapolate to unseen sequence lengths. This keeps memory and compute tractable while eliminating scale-induced distribution shifts and tiling artifacts.
